Book 9

Odysseus Reveals Himself and Begins His Story — The Cicons, the Lotus-Eaters, and the Cyclopes

Odysseus replied,

"King Alcinous, it's truly wonderful to hear a bard with a voice like a god. There's nothing better or more delightful than when everyone celebrates together. Guests sit in order, listening to the songs. Tables are piled high with bread and meat, and wine pourers keep everyone's cups full. This is the most beautiful sight a person can witness. But now you want to hear my sad story. You want me to relive those painful memories. I don't even know where to begin, or how to continue, because the gods have weighed so heavily on me."

"First, I'll tell you my name. That way, you'll know it, and perhaps one day, if I survive this time of sorrow, you might become my guests, even though I live so far away. I am Odysseus, son of Laertes. I am known throughout the human world for my wisdom and cunning, and my fame reaches the heavens. I live on the island of Ithaca. There's a tall mountain there, Mount Neriton, covered in thick forests. Nearby are several other islands, close to each other: Dulichium, Same, and the wooded island of Zacynthus. Ithaca rises highest on the western horizon, where the sun sets, while the other islands lie to the east. It's a wild and rugged island, but it raises brave men. To my eyes, no other home is more beautiful. The goddess Calypso held me captive in her cave, wanting to marry me. The cunning goddess Circe of Aeaea tried the same. But neither could persuade me. Nothing is more precious to a person than their homeland and their family. Even the grandest home in a foreign land means nothing if it's far from your parents. Now, I will tell you about the many perilous adventures I faced on my journey home from Troy, all by the will of Zeus."

"After we set sail from Troy, the winds first carried us to Ismarus, the city of the Cicons. There, I sacked the town and slaughtered its inhabitants. We took their wives and a great deal of treasure, which we divided fairly among us so no one could complain. I told my men we should leave immediately, but they foolishly refused to listen. They stayed on the beach, drinking wine and slaughtering countless sheep and cattle. Meanwhile, the Cicons called for help from other Cicons living inland. These new allies were more numerous, stronger, and skilled in warfare. They could fight from chariots or on foot, depending on the situation. So, the next morning, they swarmed like leaves and flowers in summer. The gods turned against us, and we found ourselves in deep trouble. They formed their battle lines near our ships, and both armies clashed with bronze-tipped spears. As the morning wore on, we held our ground, even though they outnumbered us. But as the sun set, when men unyoke their oxen, the Cicons overwhelmed us. We lost six men from each of our ships. In the end, only the survivors managed to escape."

"From there, we continued our voyage, our hearts heavy with grief, but grateful to have escaped death, despite losing our comrades. We didn't leave until we had called out the name of each fallen comrade three times, mourning those who perished at the hands of the Cicons. Then, Zeus unleashed a furious North wind, stirring up a hurricane. The land and sky vanished behind thick clouds, and night seemed to burst from the sky. We let our ships be driven by the gale, but the wind's force shredded our sails to ribbons. To avoid shipwreck, we lowered the sails and rowed with all our might towards land. We spent two days and two nights there, suffering from exhaustion and despair. But on the morning of the third day, we raised our masts again, hoisted our sails, and took our places, letting the wind and the helmsman guide our ship. I would have reached home safely then, if the North wind and the currents hadn't hindered me as I was rounding Cape Malea. Instead, they blew me off course near the island of Cythera."

"From there, fierce winds drove me across the sea for nine days. On the tenth day, we reached the land of the Lotus-Eaters, who eat a fruit from a flower that resembles a lotus. We landed to get fresh water, and our crew ate their lunch on the beach near the ships. After they had eaten and drunk, I sent two of my men, with a third soldier under them, to find out what kind of people lived there. They set off at once and walked among the Lotus-Eaters. The Lotus-Eaters did them no harm, but offered them lotus fruit. The fruit was so delicious that anyone who ate it forgot all about their homeland. They didn't even want to return and tell us what happened. They just wanted to stay with the Lotus-Eaters, munching on the fruit, forgetting all about going home. But even though they cried bitterly, I dragged them back to the ships and tied them securely under the benches. Then I ordered the rest of the crew to board the ships immediately, fearing that if any of them tasted the lotus, they too would lose their desire to return home. So they took their places and struck the gray sea with their oars."

"Leaving there, we continued our journey, always in great hardship. Finally, we reached the land of the lawless and heartless Cyclopes. The Cyclopes don't plant or plow. They rely on nature's bounty, eating wheat, barley, and grapes that grow wild without any farming. Their wild grapes ripen into wine, thanks to the sun and rain. They have no laws and no public gatherings. They live in caves high up on mountain peaks. Each one is the lord and master of his own family, and they don't care about their neighbors at all."

"Near the Cyclopes' harbor lies a wooded, fertile island. It's not right next to their land, but it's not far either. This island teems with wild goats. They breed in huge numbers and are never bothered by humans. Hunters, who usually brave forests and steep mountains, don't go there. It's never plowed or grazed. It remains a wild, uncultivated land, year after year, and no other living creature lives there, only goats. The Cyclopes have no ships, and no shipbuilders to make them. So they can't travel from city to city or sail across the sea to other lands, like people with ships can. If they had ships, they would have settled this island. It's so fertile and would provide everything they need in its season. There are meadows that stretch right down to the seashore in some places, well-watered and full of lush grass. Grapes would grow wonderfully there. There's flat land perfect for plowing, with deep soil that would always yield a rich harvest. There's an excellent harbor where you don't need ropes or anchors. You don't even need to moor your ship. You just beach your vessel and stay until a favorable wind blows for sailing out again. At the back of the harbor, a clear spring flows from a cave, surrounded by thick poplar trees."

"We entered that harbor, but the night was so dark, it felt as if a god guided us. We couldn't see a thing. A thick mist enveloped our ships. The moon was hidden behind thick clouds, so no one could have spotted the island even if they tried. We didn't hear any waves breaking to warn us we were near shore. Suddenly, we were just there, on land. As soon as we beached our ships, we lowered our sails, went ashore, and camped on the beach until daybreak."

When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, we admired the island and explored every part of it. The nymphs, daughters of Zeus, stirred up the wild goats so we could get meat for our supper. We brought our spears, bows, and arrows from the ships, then divided into three groups and began hunting the goats. Heaven blessed us with excellent hunting. I had twelve ships. Each ship caught nine goats, and my own ship caught ten. All day long, until sunset, we ate and drank our fill. We had plenty of wine left, because each of us had taken many jars when we plundered the city of the Cicons, and it hadn't run out yet. While we were feasting, we kept watching the land of the Cyclopes, which was nearby. We saw the smoke from their fires. We almost imagined we heard their voices and the bleating of their sheep and goats. But when the sun set and darkness fell, we camped on the beach. The next morning, I called a meeting.
"I said, 'Stay here, my brave fellows, all the rest of you. I will take my ship and explore this land myself. I want to see if they are uncivilized savages, or a welcoming and civilized people.'"

I boarded my ship, ordering my men to board and untie the ropes. They took their places and struck the gray sea with their oars. We soon reached the land, which wasn't far. There, on the face of a cliff near the sea, we saw a huge cave, draped with laurel leaves. It was a home for countless sheep and goats. There was a large yard outside, surrounded by a high wall built from stones, pine trees, and oak trees. This was the home of a giant monster, who was away, tending his flocks. He didn't associate with others. He lived alone, like an outlaw. He was a terrifying creature. He wasn't like a human at all, but more like a jagged rock cliff, towering against the sky on a high mountain peak.

I told my men to pull the ship ashore and stay put. Only the twelve bravest men would come with me. I also took a goatskin filled with sweet, dark wine. It was a gift from Maron, son of Euanthes, who was a priest of Apollo, the patron god of Ismarus. Maron lived within the temple's wooded grounds. When we were plundering the city, we respected him and spared his life, along with his wife and child. So he gave me incredibly valuable gifts: seven talents of pure gold, a silver bowl, and twelve jars of sweet, unblended wine. Its flavor was absolutely divine. No one in his household, not a servant or maid, knew about this wine. Only Maron himself, his wife, and one housekeeper knew. When he drank it, he mixed one part wine with twenty parts water. Yet, the aroma from the mixing bowl was so enchanting, it was impossible not to drink it. I filled a large goatskin with this wine and took a bag full of provisions. I had a bad feeling that I might encounter a savage, someone incredibly strong who respected neither justice nor law.

We soon reached his cave. He was out shepherding his flocks, so we went inside and examined everything we saw. His cheese racks were piled high with cheeses, and he had more lambs and kids than his pens could hold. They were separated into different groups: first the young lambs, then the older ones, and finally the tiny newborns, all kept apart. In his dairy, all the bowls, pitchers, and milk pails he used for milking were brimming with whey. When they saw all this, my men begged me to let them steal some cheeses first and take them to the ship. Then, they wanted to come back, round up the lambs and kids, load them onto the ship, and sail away. It would have been much better if we had done that, but I wouldn't listen. I hoped to meet the owner himself, thinking he might offer us a gift. However, when we finally met him, my poor men realized he was a very difficult person to deal with.

We lit a fire, offered some cheese to the gods, and ate the rest. Then we sat waiting for the Cyclops to return with his sheep. When he came, he carried an enormous load of dry firewood to light his supper fire. He threw it onto the cave floor with such a crash that we scrambled to hide in the deepest part of the cavern, trembling with fear. Meanwhile, he herded all the ewes and she-goats he intended to milk inside the cave. He left the males, both rams and he-goats, outside in the yard. Then he rolled a massive stone to block the cave entrance. It was so enormous that twenty-two strong, four-wheeled wagons wouldn't be enough to move it from the doorway. After that, he sat down and milked his ewes and goats, one by one, then let each mother nurse her young. He curdled half the milk and put it in wicker strainers. The other half he poured into bowls to drink for his supper. When he finished his work, he lit a fire. That's when he spotted us. He said:
"'Strangers, who are you? Where do you sail from? Are you traders, or are you pirates, whose hands are against everyone, and everyone's hands are against them?'"
We were terrified out of our wits by his booming voice and monstrous appearance. But I managed to speak.
'We are Achaeans on our way home from Troy,'
I said.

'But by the will of Zeus and fierce storms, we have been blown far off course. We are the followers of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, who has gained endless fame across the world by plundering such a great city and slaying countless men. Therefore, we humbly ask you to show us hospitality and give us the gifts that guests can reasonably expect. Noble sir, fear the wrath of the heavens! We are your humble petitioners. Zeus protects all honorable travelers, for he avenges all who seek refuge and all strangers in distress.'

"

He gave me a merciless answer.
'Stranger,'
he said,

'you are a fool, or you know nothing about this land. Dare you tell me to fear the gods or avoid their anger? We Cyclopes don't care about Zeus or any of your so-called blessed gods, because we are far stronger than them. I won't spare you or your companions out of any respect for Zeus, unless I feel like it. Now tell me, where did you tie up your ship when you came ashore? Is it hidden around the point, or is it right here on the coast?'

"

He said this to trick me, but I was too cunning to fall for such a trick. So I replied with a lie.
'Poseidon,'
I said,
'sent my ship onto the rocks at the far end of your land and wrecked it. We were driven onto them from the open sea. But I and those with me barely escaped the jaws of death.'

"

The cruel monster didn't answer a single word. Instead, he suddenly reached out, grabbed two of my men at once, and slammed them to the ground like puppies. Their brains splattered on the earth, soaking the ground with blood. Then he tore them apart and devoured them. He gobbled them down like a wild lion, flesh, bones, marrow, and guts, leaving nothing behind. We watched the horrifying sight, crying out and raising our hands to the heavens, completely helpless. But after Polyphemus filled his enormous belly with human flesh and washed it down with pure milk, he stretched out among his sheep and fell asleep. At first, I thought about drawing my sword and plunging it into his heart. But then I realized that if I did, we would all surely die. We could never move the massive stone the monster had placed in front of the door. So we stayed there, sobbing and sighing, until morning came.

When the rosy-fingered Dawn, goddess of morning, appeared, Polyphemus lit his fire again, skillfully milked his goats and ewes, and then reunited each mother with her young. After finishing his chores, he grabbed two more of my men and began eating them for his breakfast. A short while later, he effortlessly rolled the stone away from the door and let his sheep out. Then, he instantly put the stone back in place, as easily as closing the lid on a quiver of arrows. As soon as the stone was back, he shouted,
"Shoo, shoo!"

driving the sheep up the mountain. Now, I had to devise a plan to get my revenge and reclaim my honor.

Finally, I decided this plan would be the best. Polyphemus had a massive club lying near one of his sheep pens. It was made of green olive wood, cut to be used as a staff once it dried. The club was so huge, it was like the mast of a large merchant ship with twenty oars, big enough to sail the open seas. I approached the club and cut off about six feet of it. I gave this piece to my men and told them to smooth one end. They did as instructed, and then I sharpened the tip myself, charring it in the fire to make it even harder. After this, I hid it under the piles of dung scattered around the cave. Then, I had my men draw lots to see who would join me in driving it into the monster's eye while he slept. The lot fell to the very four men I would have chosen, making five of us in total. In the evening, the cruel monster returned with his flock. This time, he drove all the sheep inside the cave, leaving none in the yard. Perhaps it was a whim, or a god had prompted him. As soon as he put the stone back in the doorway, he sat down and skillfully milked his ewes and goats, reuniting each mother with her young. After finishing all his work, he grabbed two more of my men and ate them for his supper. So, I approached him, holding a bowl of dark wine made from ivy wood.

I said,

"Polyphemus, look here. You've eaten a lot of human flesh, so drink some of this wine. You'll see what kind of liquor we had on my ship. I brought it as an offering, hoping you'd pity me and help me on my way home. But all you do is rage and rave intolerably. You should be ashamed! How can you expect anyone to visit you again if you treat them like this?"
He took the cup and drank. He was so delighted by the wine's taste that he begged for another bowl. He said,

"Please, give me more. And tell me your name right now. I want to give you a gift you'll be happy to have. We have wine in our land too, for our soil grows grapes and the sun ripens them. But this drinks like nectar and ambrosia all in one!"
I gave him more wine. Three times I filled the bowl for him, and three times he drained it without a thought. When I saw the wine had gone to his head, I spoke to him as cleverly as I could.
"Polyphemus, if you ask my name, I will tell you. So, give me the gift you promised. My name is 'Nobody.' My father, mother, and friends have always called me that."
But the cruel monster said,
"Then I will eat all of Nobody's comrades first, and I will eat Nobody last. This is the gift I will give you!"

As soon as he finished speaking, he staggered, then fell backward, sprawling on the ground, staring up at the sky. His massive neck slumped back, and a deep sleep overcame him. Soon, he grew sick and vomited up all the wine and chunks of human flesh he had gorged on, for he was very drunk. Then, I pushed the wooden club deep into the embers to heat it until it glowed. I didn't forget to encourage my men, in case any of them lost heart. Even though it was green wood, when it was hot enough to burst into flames, I pulled it from the fire. Whether heaven filled their hearts with courage or not, my men gathered around me. We drove the sharpened end of the club into the monster's eye. Then, putting all my weight into it, I twisted it round and round. It was like two men using a wheel and strap to turn an auger, boring a hole in a ship's plank for as long as they wished. That's how we bored the red-hot club into his eye, twisting it continuously. Boiling blood frothed around it as we worked, and steam from his burning eyeball scalded his eyelids and eyebrows. The roots of his eye sizzled in the fire. Just as a blacksmith plunges an axe or hatchet into cold water to temper it, making a loud hiss, so too did Polyphemus's eye hiss around the olive wood club. His hideous screams echoed throughout the entire cave. We fled in terror, but he ripped the gore-covered club from his eye, then, mad with rage and pain, he hurled it away. As he did so, he roared out to the other Cyclopes living on the bleak headlands nearby. Hearing his cries, the Cyclopes gathered from all directions around his cave and asked what was wrong.

They called out,

"Polyphemus, what's wrong? Why are you making such a racket, breaking the night's stillness and keeping us from sleeping? Surely 'Nobody' isn't stealing your sheep? Or is 'Nobody' trying to kill you, either by trickery or by force?"
But Polyphemus roared back from inside the cave,
"'Nobody' is killing me by trickery! 'Nobody' is killing me by force!"
They replied,
"If nobody is attacking you, then you must be sick. When Zeus makes people ill, there's nothing anyone can do, so you'd better pray to your father, Poseidon."

They left, and I laughed to myself at the success of my clever trick. But the Cyclops, groaning and writhing in agony, felt around with his hands until he found the stone blocking the door and moved it aside. Then he sat in the doorway, stretching his hands out to catch anyone trying to leave with the sheep. He thought I might be foolish enough to try that.

I kept racking my brain, trying to figure out the best way to save my own life and those of my companions. Our lives depended on it, so I thought and thought. The danger was immense. Finally, I decided this plan would be the best. The male sheep were large and had heavy black fleeces. I quietly tied the sheep together in threes, using some of the vines the wicked monster used to sleep on. One man would hide under the middle sheep, with two sheep on either side covering him. So, each man was assigned three sheep. For myself, I chose a ram finer than all the others. I grabbed its back, hid myself in the thick wool under its belly. I clung stubbornly to its fleece, face upwards, holding on tight the whole time.

So, we waited in immense fear for morning to come. When Eos, the rosy-fingered goddess of dawn, appeared, the male sheep rushed out to graze. The ewes, their udders swollen to bursting, stayed in the pens, bleating and waiting to be milked. But their master, Polyphemus, despite all his pain, felt the backs of all the sheep as they stood upright. He wasn't sharp enough to realize that men were hidden beneath their bellies. Finally, as the ram, heavy with its thick fleece and my cunning self hidden beneath, was about to leave, Polyphemus grabbed it and said,

"My good ram, why are you the last to leave my cave this morning? You're never one to let the ewes go before you. You always led the flock, whether to flowery meadows or bubbling springs, and you were always the first to return home at night. But now you lag behind everyone. Is it because you know your master has lost his eye, and you're sorry that that wicked 'Nobody' and his terrible crew got me drunk and blinded me? But I will surely take his life yet. If only you could understand and speak, you would tell me where that wretched man is hiding. Then I would smash his brains on the ground until they splattered all over the cave. That way, I would get some satisfaction for the harm this good-for-nothing 'Nobody' has done to me!"

As he spoke, he drove the ram outside. Once we were a little way from the cave and the pens, I first slipped out from under the ram's belly, then freed my comrades. The sheep were very fat, and by constantly guiding them in the right direction, we managed to drive them down to the ship. The crew rejoiced greatly at seeing those of us who had escaped death, but they wept for our other comrades killed by the Cyclops. However, I nodded and frowned, signaling them to stop their crying. I ordered them to load all the sheep onto the ship at once and set out to sea. They boarded, took their places, and struck the gray sea with their oars. When we were far enough that my voice would carry, I began to taunt the Cyclops.

I shouted,

"Cyclops, you should have known what kind of man you were dealing with before you ate my comrades in your cave! You wretch, eating visitors in your own home? You should have known your sin would catch up to you. Now Zeus and the other gods have punished you!"

He grew more and more furious as he heard me. He tore the top off a high mountain and flung it right in front of my ship. It barely missed the end of the rudder. The sea quaked as the rock crashed into it, and the wave it created pushed us back towards the mainland, forcing us toward the shore. But I grabbed a long pole and pushed the ship away. I nodded, signaling my men to row for their lives. They then rowed with all their might. When we had gone twice as far as before, I wanted to taunt the Cyclops again. But my men begged and pleaded with me to keep quiet.

They cried out,

"Please, don't be crazy enough to provoke this savage creature any further! He already threw one rock at us that drove us back to the mainland, and we thought we were dead then. If he had heard any more voices then, he would have smashed our heads and our ship's hull into jelly with the jagged rocks he would have hurled at us. He can throw rocks a long, long way!"
But I wouldn't listen to them. In my rage, I shouted to him,
"Cyclops, if anyone asks who put out your eye and ruined your sight, tell them it was Odysseus, son of Laertes, the valiant warrior who lives in Ithaca!"
Polyphemus groaned and cried out,

"Oh no! The old prophecy about me is actually coming true. There once was a brave, giant prophet here, Telemus, son of Eurymus. He was an excellent seer who made prophecies for the Cyclopes until he grew old. He told me that one day this would happen, and I would lose my eye to Odysseus. I always expected someone grand and super-strong, but instead, it's just a pathetic weakling who blinded me by taking advantage of me when I was drunk! Odysseus, come here. I'll give you gifts of hospitality, and I'll ask Poseidon to help you on your journey. Poseidon is my father, after all. If he wishes, he can heal me. No one else, god or human, can do that."
Then I said,
"I wish I could be as sure of killing you right now and sending you to Hades' house, as I am sure that Poseidon can't heal your eye!"
Polyphemus lifted his hands to the sky and prayed,

"Great Poseidon, if I am truly your son, then let Odysseus never return home alive. But if he must reach his friends eventually, let him do so late and in a terrible state, after losing all his men. Let him arrive home on another's ship and find only suffering in his house."

As Polyphemus prayed, Poseidon heard his plea. Then, the Cyclops picked up a rock much larger than the first one. He swung it over his head and hurled it with immense power. The rock landed just in front of our ship, barely missing the end of the rudder. When the rock hit the sea, the water churned violently. The powerful wave it created pushed our ship further towards the island's shore.

Finally, we reached the island where we had left our other ships. Our comrades were waiting anxiously, mourning us and fearing the worst. We pulled our ship onto the sandy beach and disembarked. We also brought the Cyclops' sheep ashore and divided them fairly among everyone, so no one had reason to complain. My companions agreed that I should have the ram as a special share. So, on the beach, I sacrificed the ram and burned its thigh bones as an offering to Zeus, the lord of all. But Zeus did not accept my sacrifice. Instead, he was already planning how to destroy both my ships and my comrades.

We spent the entire day feasting on meat and wine until the sun went down. When darkness fell, we camped on the beach. As rosy-fingered Dawn, the goddess of morning, appeared, I ordered my men to board the ships and untie the ropes. Each man took his place and rowed hard across the grey sea. We carried the sorrow of losing our comrades in our hearts, but we also felt relief at escaping death, and so we continued our journey.
